title: Wooden Roller Coasters
description: Wooden roller coasters are coasters whose track structure is built principally from wood, with steel running rails on top of a wooden stack. They are known for a particular ride feel: the structure flexes slightly, the train rattles and rumbles, and the drops deliver strong airtime, the floating feeling as the train crests a hill. Classic wooden coasters use out-and-back or twister layouts, with long drops, bunny hills, and banked turns. NEW examples operating today include the Beast at Kings Island in Ohio, a long terrain coaster, and the Cyclone at Coney Island in New York, a 1927 classic. PAST examples include the Bobs at Riverview Park in Chicago, retired when that park closed in 1967, and the Starliner at Miracle Strip, later relocated rather than lost. Wooden coasters remain beloved because no two ride exactly alike.

demo.code:
DROPS = [("First drop", 35), ("Second hill", 22), ("Bunny hills", 12), ("Twister finale", 18)]
print("Wooden coaster classifier: airtime score")
total = 0
for name, height in DROPS:
    score = height * 2
    total += score
    print("%s: drop %d m, airtime score %d" % (name, height, score))
print("Total airtime score: %d" % total)
print("Classification: wooden coaster (wood structure, steel running rails)")
print("Operating examples: Beast (NEW), Cyclone (NEW); retired: Bobs (PAST)")
demo.expected_output:
Wooden coaster classifier: airtime score
First drop: drop 35 m, airtime score 70
Second hill: drop 22 m, airtime score 44
Bunny hills: drop 12 m, airtime score 24
Twister finale: drop 18 m, airtime score 36
Total airtime score: 174
Classification: wooden coaster (wood structure, steel running rails)
Operating examples: Beast (NEW), Cyclone (NEW); retired: Bobs (PAST)

title: Steel Roller Coasters
description: Steel roller coasters are coasters built with tubular or box steel track on steel supports, which allows smoother curves, steeper drops, inversions, and more precise shapes than wood. They range from family coasters with gentle hills to hypercoasters over 60 meters tall and gigacoasters over 90 meters. NEW examples operating today include Millennium Force at Cedar Point in Ohio, a steel giga-style coaster, and countless steel loopers at parks worldwide. PAST examples include early steel coasters retired as parks modernized, such as the original steel loopers of the 1970s that were replaced by taller, faster successors. Steel is now the dominant coaster material, and its precision is what makes inversions and launches practical at scale.

title: Inverted Coasters
description: Inverted coasters are steel coasters where the train hangs beneath the track, so riders' legs dangle free and the track passes overhead. The type became famous in the 1990s with rides that thread riders through loops, rolls, and dives with nothing below their feet. NEW examples operating today include the Batman-style inverted coasters at several Six Flags parks and Raptor at Cedar Point in Ohio. PAST examples include early inverted coasters removed as parks redeveloped, such as smaller inverted models retired from parks that have since closed. The sensation is distinct: the world swings beneath you, and every inversion feels closer because there is no floor.

demo.code:
ELEMENTS = ["Lift hill", "First drop", "Vertical loop", "Zero-g roll", "Corkscrew", "Brake run"]
print("Inverted coaster element counter")
print("Elements in this layout: %d" % len(ELEMENTS))
for i, e in enumerate(ELEMENTS, 1):
    print("%d. %s (train hangs below the track)" % (i, e))
print("Inversions counted: %d" % 3)
print("Classification: inverted coaster (hanging train, legs free)")

title: Launched Coasters
description: Launched coasters replace the traditional lift hill with a launch: a burst of acceleration, by magnetic, hydraulic, or tire drive, that fires the train from a standstill to full speed in seconds. Launches allow coasters to start with a sprint, to cross top hats, and to run courses that never climb a lift. NEW examples operating today include Top Thrill-style strata coasters and modern multi-launch coasters such as VelociCoaster at Universal Orlando. PAST examples include early launched coasters retired after short lives, such as some of the first hydraulic launches that proved hard to maintain. The launch is the signature moment: a countdown, a jolt, and then the fastest part of the ride comes first.

demo.code:
LAUNCH_SPEED = 120
LAUNCH_TIME = 2.4
accel = LAUNCH_SPEED / 3.6 / LAUNCH_TIME
print("Launched coaster launch math")
print("Launch speed: %d km/h in %.1f seconds" % (LAUNCH_SPEED, LAUNCH_TIME))
print("Average acceleration: %.1f m/s^2 (about %.1f g)" % (accel, accel / 9.81))
print("Classification: launched coaster (no lift hill; acceleration launch)")
print("Operating example: VelociCoaster (NEW); retired: early hydraulic launches (PAST)")

title: Dark Rides

They range from gentle family journeys through fairy tales to elaborate adventures with moving figures and special effects. NEW examples operating today include Pirates of the Caribbean at Disney parks, a boat journey through pirate scenes, and the Haunted Mansion, a gentle ghost story told through effects. PAST examples include older dark rides retired with their parks, such as the classic pretzel-style dark rides of mid-century American parks. The dark is the point: it hides the machinery, focuses attention on the scene, and lets a small space feel like a whole world.

title: Log Flumes
description: Log flumes are water rides where riders sit in hollow log-shaped boats that float along a channel and climb lift hills before plunging down drops, ending with a splash. The final drop is the payoff: a steep descent into a lagoon that throws up a sheet of spray. NEW examples operating today include Splash Mountain-style log flumes (now rethemed at some parks) and Timber Mountain Log Run at Knott's Berry Farm. PAST examples include the log flumes of closed parks, such as the flume at Euclid Beach Park, retired when that park closed in 1969. Log flumes are summer staples: gentle drifting punctuated by one or two big splashes.

title: River Rapids Rides
description: River rapids rides are circular-raft water rides where a round raft carrying several riders spins and drifts down a fast-flowing artificial river with rapids, waves, and waterfalls. Unlike log flumes, which follow a fixed channel, rafts rotate freely, so every ride is different and nobody knows who will get soaked. NEW examples operating today include Kali River Rapids at Disney's Animal Kingdom and Grizzly River Run at Disney California Adventure. PAST examples include rapids rides removed from parks that closed or redeveloped their water areas, such as the rapids rides of the former Opryland USA. The appeal is social: the whole raft shares the soaking.

title: Ferris Wheels
description: Ferris wheels are giant vertical wheels with passenger gondolas mounted around the rim, turning slowly so riders rise high above the park and see the whole site spread out below. They are among the oldest amusement rides, invented for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, and they remain park landmarks: a wheel on the skyline says 'amusement park' from miles away. NEW examples operating today include the Wonder Wheel at Coney Island, a 1920 classic with sliding cars, and the High Roller in Las Vegas, one of the world's tallest observation wheels. PAST examples include the original 1893 Ferris wheel itself, dismantled after its fairs, and the wheels of closed parks such as Riverview's. The wheel is the park's slow ride: gentle, high, and best at sunset.

title: Carousels
description: Carousels are rotating platforms with rows of carved horses and other figures that rise and fall on poles as the platform turns, accompanied by band organ music. They are the oldest surviving amusement ride type and the most artistic: carousel horses were carved by master workshops, painted in bright colors, and collected as folk art when parks closed. NEW examples operating today include the historic carousels still running at parks and the Bryant Park carousel in New York. PAST examples include the carousel at Euclid Beach Park, whose figures survive in museums, and the carousels of closed parks whose horses were auctioned to collectors. A carousel ride is short and gentle, but the craft repays a close look: every horse is a small sculpture.

title: Drop Towers
description: Drop towers are tall vertical rides that lift riders high into the air and then drop them, using brakes to stop the fall with a rush of air and a stomach-drop feeling. Some towers launch riders upward first; some drop repeatedly in a bouncing pattern; all of them trade on height and the moment of release. NEW examples operating today include the Tower of Terror-style drop rides and the Zumanjaro-style towers attached to coasters. PAST examples include early parachute towers, such as the Parachute Jump at Coney Island, now a landmark rather than a ride, and the parachute tower at Riverview Park, retired with that park in 1967. The drop is short but intense: the anticipation on the way up is half the ride.

demo.code:
import math
HEIGHT_M = 60
print("Drop tower fall estimator")
print("Tower height: %d m" % HEIGHT_M)
fall_time = math.sqrt(2 * HEIGHT_M / 9.81)
print("Free-fall time (physics, no air resistance): %.2f seconds" % fall_time)
print("Speed at brake point (illustrative, braked before ground): about %.0f km/h" % (9.81 * fall_time * 3.6 * 0.8))
print("Classification: drop tower (vertical lift, braked drop)")
demo.expected_output:
Drop tower fall estimator
Tower height: 60 m
Free-fall time (physics, no air resistance): 3.50 seconds
Speed at brake point (illustrative, braked before ground): about 99 km/h
Classification: drop tower (vertical lift, braked drop)

title: Spinning Flat Rides

NEW examples operating today include the Teacups at Disney parks, the Scrambler at countless fairs and parks, and modern frisbee pendulums at major parks. PAST examples include the spinning rides of closed parks, such as the Tilt-A-Whirl and Rotor rides that once filled midways and have since been retired as parks modernized. Spinning rides reward repeat riding: the same ride feels different depending on where you sit.

title: Mine Trains
description: Mine trains are family coasters themed as mine cars that race through tunnels, over trestles, and around mountains, with moderate drops and turns rather than extreme height or inversions. title: Monorails and People Movers
description: Monorails and people movers are transport rides: elevated trains or slow-moving vehicles that carry guests around a park or resort, doubling as both transportation and a gentle sightseeing ride. Monorails run on a single beam, high above the ground, giving riders a sweeping view of the park; people movers run on a track at lower height with continuous boarding. NEW examples operating today include the Walt Disney World Monorail, linking parks and resorts, and the Tomorrowland Transit Authority PeopleMover at Magic Kingdom. PAST examples include the monorails and people movers of closed parks and world's fairs, such as the monorail at the former Opryland USA area and fair monorails dismantled after their expos. They are the park's calm ride: no drops, no scares, just the view.
